title: A Convergence Analysis of the Random Feature Method for Linear PDEs
authors: Jingrun Chen, Yixin Luo, Xiaojun Peng
abstract: The Random Feature Method (RFM) distinguishes itself among machine learning approaches to partial differential equations (PDEs) through its superior accuracy and computational efficiency. Nevertheless, the theoretical underpinnings of RFM remain incompletely elucidated. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of RFM within the framework of kernel methods, focusing on two principal aspects: (i) approximation by finitely many random features in Sobolev norms and the PDE residual seminorm, and (ii) estimation over the induced reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) from finitely many noiseless collocation observations. We relate both problems to kernel ridge regression (KRR) and establish upper and lower bounds in terms of the eigenvalues of the associated integral operators under the respective assumptions. Combining the approximation and estimation lower bounds, we establish a lower bound under simultaneous restrictions on the numbers of random features and collocation observations. We further quantify how activation regularity affects these eigenvalues, obtaining algebraic upper bounds for finitely smooth activations and stretched-exponential upper bounds for analytic activations.

infographic.key_insight: A kernel-method analysis links random feature and collocation budgets to convergence bounds for solving linear PDEs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The theory helps characterize how feature count, collocation count, and activation smoothness constrain PDE solution accuracy.
method: Analyze finite random-feature approximation in Sobolev norms and the PDE residual seminorm.
Relate approximation and noiseless RKHS collocation estimation to kernel ridge regression.
Derive eigenvalue-based upper and lower bounds, including a joint resource lower bound.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical bounds rather than numerical benchmarks, with algebraic eigenvalue upper bounds for finitely smooth activations and stretched-exponential bounds for analytic activations.
infographic.watch_item: The estimation analysis assumes noiseless collocation observations; applicability to noisy data requires separate justification.
infographic.paper_title: A Convergence Analysis of the Random Feature Method for Linear PDEs

title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research
authors: Yang Chen, Qianyi Wang, Ronghui Yang, Zhanhao Li, Yu Cong, Chen Zhang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems. This progress is ushering mathematics into an era of proof abundance, raising a fundamental challenge: how can we ensure the correctness of the ever-growing volume of AI-generated proofs and transform them into trustworthy, machine-verified mathematical knowledge? We introduce Turing Agent, an agent harness designed to orchestrate end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics. Its wo-scale architecture integrates theorem formalization and proof formalization agents, empowered by structured proof decomposition, parallel verification, accumulated proof experience, and selective semantic review. Leveraging our collaborations with theoretical computer science (TCS) researchers, we focus our evaluation on TCS, a particularly demanding domain characterized by intricate quantification, complex dependencies, and stringent semantic requirements. Against direct generation and general-purpose coding harnesses, including Codex CLI and Claude Code, Turing Agent achieves approximately 57-62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused subset of RLMEval, using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Notably, Turing Agent, built on DeepSeek, successfully completes the formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks from OpenAI's October 2026 collection. One particularly challenging TCS problem required about a hundred formally verified auxiliary claims. Moreover, by actively exploring and refining the formalization process, Turing Agent can uncover simpler alternative proofs, expose unnecessary dependencies in original proofs, and generate reusable mathematical knowledge as a byproduct of verification.

infographic.key_insight: Turing Agent orchestrates end-to-end formal verification of research mathematics, turning AI-generated proofs into machine-checked knowledge.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A two-scale agent architecture offers a practical approach to coordinating theorem translation, proof construction, and verification across complex mathematical dependencies.
method: Coordinate theorem-formalization and proof-formalization agents.
Decompose proofs into auxiliary claims and verify them in parallel.
Reuse accumulated proof experience and selectively review semantic fidelity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports approximately 57–62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench, 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused RLMEval subset, and verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Machine-checked proofs still require semantic scrutiny to ensure the formal statement faithfully represents the intended mathematics; evaluation focuses on theoretical computer science.
infographic.paper_title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research

title: Rethinking Supervision Scaling in On-Policy Distillation: From Dense Supervision to Stochastic Horizons
authors: Xinhao Yao, Zhenxing Dou, Yong Liu
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision along student-generated trajectories, yet the learning benefits of longer trajectories may not scale proportionally with their computational cost. We investigate how supervision utility evolves with trajectory length. Controlled experiments reveal diminishing returns from additional supervised tokens, while showing that later positions remain learnable and exhibit substantial cross-position supervision transfer. Gradient analysis further identifies shared update components across response positions and diverse position-specific residuals whose cross-rollout consistency decreases at greater depths. Motivated by these findings, we propose Stochastic Horizons On-Policy Distillation (SH-OPD), which reduces redundant supervision by randomly varying rollout horizons while preserving access to deeper response states. SH-OPD samples a shared horizon for each training batch, enabling efficient parallel generation without per-sequence horizon scheduling overhead. We characterize the resulting reweighting bias and derive a compute-reweighting trade-off under standard optimization assumptions. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation demonstrate that SH-OPD achieves slightly higher mathematical reasoning accuracy at approximately 45% of the per-update cost of standard OPD, while maintaining competitive code generation performance at around 60% of the baseline cost. These results highlight the benefits of efficient supervision allocation across response depths.

infographic.key_insight: Longer on-policy distillation trajectories yield diminishing supervision returns, while randomly varying rollout horizons can preserve learning from deeper response states at lower cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Batch-shared stochastic horizons reduce per-update compute while retaining efficient parallel generation without per-sequence horizon scheduling.
method: Analyze supervision utility, cross-position transfer, and gradient structure across response depths.
Randomly sample one shared rollout horizon per training batch to reduce redundant supervision.
Characterize horizon-induced reweighting bias and derive a compute–reweighting trade-off.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments report slightly higher mathematical reasoning accuracy at approximately 45% of standard OPD's per-update cost, with competitive code generation performance at around 60% of baseline cost.
infographic.watch_item: Random horizons reweight supervision across response depths; lower per-update cost does not by itself establish lower total training cost.
infographic.paper_title: Rethinking Supervision Scaling in On-Policy Distillation: From Dense Supervision to Stochastic Horizons

title: Second scaling regime in high-dimensional function approximation and curse of dimensionality
authors: Shukai Du, Thu Le, Samuel N. Stechmann
abstract: High-dimensional function approximation is often subject to the curse of dimensionality, commonly described by a hypercube scaling regime with a large expense of $R^d$ grid points, where $R$ denotes the side length of a hypercube in $d$ dimensions. Here we show that a second scaling regime, which we call the lattice ball scaling regime, also arises and is relevant for practical applications. In this regime, the expense scales as $d^{R^2}/(R^2!)$ and therefore grows polynomially with $d$. This regime arises without additional special assumptions of special types of function spaces or error norms. The lattice ball scaling regime occurs when $R^2\ll d$, due to the discrete nature of counting the expense as the number of lattice points inside a hypersphere. Here we investigate this regime, which arises from the classical problem of approximating high-dimensional functions from common spaces of analytic or $m$-times continuously differentiable functions using orthogonal series (spectral method) such as Fourier, Chebyshev, and Legendre polynomial series. For many applications, the expense in the lattice ball scaling regime can be substantially smaller than that of the hypercube scaling regime, making accurate approximations more accessible. Numerical illustrations include classifying images of handwritten digits from the MNIST dataset and learning the solution operators of partial differential equations, such as Burgers' equation and the radiative transfer equation. The potential for connections with artificial neural networks and other machine learning methods is also discussed.

infographic.key_insight: High-dimensional function approximation admits a lattice-ball regime with expense scaling as d^(R²)/(R²!), polynomial in dimension d for fixed R, when R² ≪ d.
infographic.engineering_relevance: In this regime, spectral approximations can require substantially fewer terms than hypercube scaling R^d suggests, potentially reducing high-dimensional modeling costs.
method: Approximate analytic or m-times continuously differentiable functions using orthogonal series.
Use Fourier, Chebyshev, or Legendre expansions.
Analyze expense by counting lattice points inside a hypersphere.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical illustrations cover MNIST digit classification and learning solution operators for Burgers’ and radiative transfer equations; the abstract reports no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The favorable scaling requires R² ≪ d and does not imply dimension-independent cost or removal of the curse in every approximation regime.
infographic.paper_title: Second scaling regime in high-dimensional function approximation and curse of dimensionality

title: Explicit Regularization for Flow Matching
authors: Lars Ruthotto, Eran Treister
abstract: Learning the underlying probability distribution from samples is a core problem in statistics and applied mathematics. Generative models based on diffusion and flow matching learn a velocity field whose flow transports a known distribution to the data distribution. They produce novel, realistic samples, although the empirical learning problem is ill posed near the data distribution. Its minimizer transports the samples onto the training data, and small perturbations of the data change the velocity field strongly near the end of the flow. The observed generalization is often attributed to implicit regularization by the network parameterization, early stopping of the training, and the time integration during sampling. Explicit regularization has advanced the theory and computation of many inverse problems and has recently been proposed to prevent memorization in generative models. With a regularizer on the magnitude of the velocity, however, the field approaches the memorizing velocity unless the regularization parameter grows to infinity fast enough, and it then stays bounded by a constant that is small only for large parameters. We show that penalizing the derivatives of order $k$ of the velocity renders the $D$-dimensional empirical problem well posed uniformly in time if $2k > D$ and the training points are in general position. Our experiments in one and two dimensions discretize the velocity with splines and use direct solvers for the regularized least-squares problems to exclude optimization error. Refining the discretization in space and time changes the error of the Hessian-regularized flows only marginally, whereas without the regularizer the error tends to that of memorization. These flows generalize, with errors comparable to or lower than those of well-tuned kernel density estimates.

infographic.key_insight: Penalizing order-k derivatives of the velocity makes empirical flow matching uniformly well posed in time when 2k > D and training points are in general position.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Explicit derivative regularization offers a principled way to stabilize flow matching against memorization and sensitivity to discretization.
method: Regularize velocity derivatives rather than velocity magnitude alone.
Discretize velocity fields with splines in one and two dimensions.
Use direct solvers for regularized least squares to exclude optimization error.
infographic.evidence_signal: In 1D and 2D experiments, Hessian-regularized flows showed only marginal error changes under space-time refinement and achieved errors comparable to or lower than well-tuned kernel density estimates.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to low-dimensional spline models; the condition 2k > D requires higher-order derivative penalties as dimension increases.
infographic.paper_title: Explicit Regularization for Flow Matching

title: PISG: Constraint-Aligned Signal Amplification for Diffusion-Based Combinatorial Optimization
authors: Yuming Zhang, Xianchen Zhou, Hongxia Wang
abstract: Diffusion-based solvers have become a prominent approach to neural combinatorial optimization. At inference time, they assign each decision variable a prediction score. A greedy decoder ranks candidates by these scores and checks hard constraints to ensure feasibility. Top-ranked candidates should be both promising and jointly feasible, making prediction-constraint alignment critical. When this alignment is weak, greedy decoding skips constraint-violating candidates and falls back to lower-ranked alternatives, degrading solution quality. Existing test-time methods improve search, sampling, or decoding, but do not directly strengthen this alignment before decoding. We observe that trained denoisers already carry constraint-aligned structural signals. Building on this observation, we propose Perturbed Instance-Structure Guidance (PISG), a training-free method that amplifies these signals at test time. At each denoising step, PISG constructs a structure-degraded prediction and extrapolates the unperturbed prediction away from it. The resulting guided prediction improves candidate rankings before constrained decoding. Signal analysis shows that this guidance concentrates on constraint-critical variables rather than uniformly rescaling scores. Under greedy decoding and without downstream refinement, PISG improves all 16 TSP solver-scale pairs across DIFUSCO, T2T, FastT2T, and StruDiCO, and all four MIS-ER solvers, with MIS-ER solved-cost gains up to +4.8%. The gains persist on most large-scale settings after 2-opt, and a preliminary study extends PISG to a Transformer-based solver. These results identify prediction-constraint alignment as an effective test-time enhancement direction for diffusion-based combinatorial optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/Ming-321/PISG.

infographic.key_insight: PISG improves diffusion-based combinatorial optimization by amplifying constraint-aligned prediction signals before greedy decoding.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This training-free inference method improves candidate rankings for constrained optimization without retraining the solver or relying on downstream refinement.
method: Construct a structure-degraded prediction at each denoising step.
Extrapolate the unperturbed prediction away from the degraded prediction.
Apply constrained greedy decoding to the guided scores.
infographic.evidence_signal: Without downstream refinement, PISG improved all 16 tested TSP solver-scale pairs and all four MIS-ER solvers, with MIS-ER solved-cost gains up to 4.8%.
infographic.watch_item: Inference overhead is not quantified in the abstract, and evidence for Transformer-based solvers remains preliminary.
infographic.paper_title: PISG: Constraint-Aligned Signal Amplification for Diffusion-Based Combinatorial Optimization

title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations
authors: Yuan Qiu, Wolfgang Dahmen, Peng Chen
abstract: Physics-informed operator learning trains neural operators on the residual of a parametric partial differential equation (PDE) instead of labeled solution data, but its reliability depends on a variationally correct residual: one that is equivalent to the error in a norm dictated by the equation, the PDE-compliant norm. For nonlinear equations written as first-order systems, we prove that the first-order system least-squares residual is equivalent to the error in this norm near a solution branch if the linearized residual is stable and the residual derivative is Lipschitz continuous, possibly in a norm stronger than the error norm. We verify these conditions for monotone reaction, solution- and gradient-dependent diffusion, and compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity. The stability mechanisms vary across these classes, as do the regions where the equivalence holds, from arbitrary bounded sets to a neighborhood of the branch. In a conforming finite element space, we show that the loss excess of a state near the finite element solution is equivalent to its squared distance from that solution. We use this loss to train a reduced basis neural operator with values in this space, with solution snapshots needed only for the basis and the loss and its symbolically derived gradient assembled by the finite element library. At inference, this loss estimates the error. Numerically, the square root of the loss excess tracks the error within factors comparable to those of the linear case, and the operator achieves higher accuracy in the PDE-compliant norm than grid-based baselines evaluated in the same finite element space.

infographic.key_insight: For nonlinear PDEs, a first-order system least-squares residual can reliably measure solution error in the PDE-compliant norm under stability and smoothness conditions near a solution branch.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables physics-informed neural operators with equation-aligned training losses and inference-time error indicators, without requiring labeled solutions for residual training.
method: Establish residual–error equivalence using linearized stability and Lipschitz continuity of the residual derivative.
Verify conditions for monotone reaction, nonlinear diffusion, and compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity.
Train a reduced-basis neural operator in a conforming finite element space, using snapshots for the basis and finite element assembly for the loss and gradient.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests show that the square root of loss excess tracks error within factors comparable to the linear case, while the operator outperforms grid-based baselines in the PDE-compliant norm when evaluated in the same finite element space.
infographic.watch_item: Residual–error guarantees depend on the PDE and admissible region; some require proximity to a solution branch and regularity measured in a stronger norm.
infographic.paper_title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations

title: From Objective Compromise to Structure-Enabled Intelligence: Reshaping the Scientific Paradigm of AI
authors: Shengchang Chen
abstract: Mainstream artificial intelligence systems, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), are fundamentally constructed upon the Optimization-Driven (OD) paradigm. This paradigm can be characterized as an ill-posed optimization problem within a high-dimensional parameter space. When confronted with real-world scenarios characterized by noise and conflicting constraints, the logic of global error minimization inherently induces a strong smoothing effect. Consequently, this yields statistical compromise solutions that flatten local features, making it arduous to overcome the inherent bottleneck of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization. Existing AI models generate outputs purely based on statistical probabilities. They lack the capacity to autonomously discern truth from falsehood or establish causal logic, thereby lacking genuine cognitive intelligence. To address the ontological limitations of the OD paradigm, this paper proposes a novel paradigm termed \textit{Structure-Enabled Intelligence}. This approach abandons the conventional path of relying solely on computing power scaling and data fitting to achieve emergent intelligence. Instead, it embeds mathematical structures and physical mechanisms as underlying priors into the algorithmic architecture, constraining the model's solving process with structured scientific rules. Through this paradigm shift from ``data-driven objective fitting'' to ``mechanism-structure dominance,'' the proposed approach fundamentally mitigates the issue of statistical compromise, enhances the model's extrapolation and generalization capabilities, and simultaneously reshapes human-AI synergy by upholding human subjectivity in scientific cognition.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes replacing optimization-dominated statistical fitting with structure-enabled intelligence that embeds mathematical and physical rules into model architectures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For scientific AI, structural priors could improve constraint adherence and out-of-distribution generalization beyond what data fitting alone provides.
method: Frame optimization-driven AI as prone to smoothing and compromise under noisy, conflicting constraints.
Embed mathematical structures and physical mechanisms as architectural priors.
Constrain inference with scientific rules while preserving human oversight in scientific reasoning.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a conceptual proposal but reports no datasets, benchmarks, quantitative results, or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits remain unverified in the abstract, and incorrect or overly restrictive structural priors could limit model applicability.
infographic.paper_title: From Objective Compromise to Structure-Enabled Intelligence: Reshaping the Scientific Paradigm of AI

title: CompCert4Lean: Porting a Verified C Compiler to Lean in Six Weeks with Parallel Coding Agents
authors: Cong Wang, Zhiyang Chen, Fan Long, Martin Rinard
abstract: We present CompCert4Lean, a large-scale port of CompCert 3.17's verified compiler core from Rocq to Lean, completed in approximately six weeks by one expert directing parallel LLM agents. Our migration workflow partitions the development along its dependencies, audits translated definitions and theorem statements before large-scale proof reconstruction, and then reconstructs proofs in parallel against stable interfaces. The resulting compiler covers typed CompCert C through x86-64 assembly, discharges all 4,908 recorded proof obligations without project-specific axioms, and produces executable Linux binaries. The workflow enabled the expert to concentrate on organizing the work rather than supplying technical solutions. Of 1,071 human interactions, 88.8% concerned workflow and coordination, while only three supplied technical direction. Optimization campaigns further demonstrate the benefit of the Lean port for agent-driven verified development. Under matched budgets of 24 active hours, GPT-6-astra produced a Lean candidate with 11.7% lower generated-program runtime across 29 small-tests programs, compared with 2.3% lower for its Rocq candidate, both relative to original CompCert 3.17 and while preserving the end-to-end correctness theorem. These results show that parallel LLM agents can support large-scale migration with limited human technical direction and subsequently improve the migrated compiler while retaining its formal guarantees.

infographic.key_insight: One expert directing parallel LLM agents ported CompCert’s verified compiler core from Rocq to Lean in about six weeks, completing all 4,908 recorded proof obligations without project-specific axioms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The port demonstrates a path to agent-assisted maintenance and optimization of a formally verified compiler while retaining its end-to-end correctness theorem.
method: Partition the migration along dependency boundaries.
Audit translated definitions and theorem statements before rebuilding proofs.
Reconstruct proofs in parallel against stable interfaces.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 29 small-tests programs and matched 24-active-hour budgets, GPT-6-astra’s Lean candidate reduced generated-program runtime by 11.7% versus original CompCert 3.17, compared with 2.3% for its Rocq candidate.
infographic.watch_item: The optimization evidence comes from 29 small test programs, so performance gains may not generalize to larger production workloads.
infographic.paper_title: CompCert4Lean: Porting a Verified C Compiler to Lean in Six Weeks with Parallel Coding Agents

title: Structure-Preserving Neural Time-Stepping for Gradient-Flow PDEs via Onsager's Variational Principle
authors: Zhonghua Qiao, Xianmin Xu, Rukang You, Tao Zhou
abstract: We propose a unified Onsager-based neural time-stepping (ONTS) framework for solving gradient-flow partial differential equations with conserved and nonconserved dynamics. Unlike conventional neural time-stepping methods that directly parameterize the evolving state, the proposed framework employs spatial neural networks to approximate the Onsager process variables, namely, the rates in nonconserved systems and the fluxes in conserved systems. Within this Eulerian framework, we develop three complementary schemes: an explicit least-squares scheme (E-ONTS), an implicit variational scheme (I-ONTS), and a predictor--corrector scheme (PC-ONTS) that combines explicit prediction with safeguarded implicit correction. For conserved systems, the flux-based formulation guarantees discrete mass conservation under periodic or no-flux boundary conditions. Furthermore, we rigorously establish unconditional discrete energy stability for the implicit schemes, provided that a suitable descent criterion is satisfied, without requiring global minimization of the neural variational objective. Numerical experiments for the heat, Allen--Cahn, Cahn--Hilliard, Fokker--Planck, and coupled Poisson--Nernst--Planck equations demonstrate the accuracy, robustness, and structure-preserving properties of the proposed framework.

infographic.key_insight: Learning rates or fluxes instead of evolving states enables neural PDE time-stepping that preserves gradient-flow structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a structure-preserving approach to simulating diffusion, phase-field dynamics, and coupled transport systems.
method: Use spatial neural networks to approximate Onsager rates for nonconserved dynamics and fluxes for conserved dynamics.
Advance solutions with explicit least-squares, implicit variational, or predictor–corrector schemes.
Preserve discrete mass under periodic or no-flux boundaries and ensure unconditional discrete energy stability for implicit schemes satisfying a descent criterion.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on heat, Allen–Cahn, Cahn–Hilliard, Fokker–Planck, and coupled Poisson–Nernst–Planck equations demonstrate accuracy, robustness, and structure preservation.
infographic.watch_item: Implicit energy stability depends on satisfying the required descent criterion during neural optimization; it is not guaranteed for arbitrary training outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: Structure-Preserving Neural Time-Stepping for Gradient-Flow PDEs via Onsager's Variational Principle

title: Physics-informed neural network for model-based global computation of the asymptotic phase of limit-cycle oscillators
authors: Petar Mircheski, Hiroya Nakao
abstract: The asymptotic phase is the central object of phase reduction theory for limit-cycle oscillators. It is a scalar coordinate defined throughout the basin of attraction of a limit cycle that advances at a constant natural frequency along every trajectory. Computing the phase from a given mathematical model requires solving a first-order partial differential equation (PDE) over the entire basin, which is challenging due to high computation costs and complex boundary conditions. In this study, we propose a physics-informed neural network to efficiently calculate the asymptotic phase of limit-cycle oscillators. By incorporating three types of loss functions, we train a physics-informed neural network (PINN) to satisfy the governing PDE for the asymptotic phase and the adjoint equation for the phase gradient. The trained network delivers the phase function accurately and, via automatic differentiation, allows the calculation of the phase gradient governing the oscillator's response to perturbations, which enables rapid entrainment closed-loop control using strong inputs. We validate the approach using three types of limit-cycle oscillators and demonstrate that the PINN can facilitate fast and global phase-locking control.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-informed neural network learns the asymptotic phase of limit-cycle oscillators across their basin of attraction, supporting phase-based control.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The learned phase and its gradient enable fast phase-locking feedback control, including entrainment with strong inputs.
method: Learn the phase function from a mathematical oscillator model using a PINN.
Combine three loss types to enforce the phase PDE and the adjoint equation for its gradient.
Use automatic differentiation to obtain phase gradients for feedback control.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports validation on three types of limit-cycle oscillators and demonstrations of fast, global phase-locking control.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy across the full basin and under strong inputs should be checked; the abstract provides no quantitative error or runtime benchmarks.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-informed neural network for model-based global computation of the asymptotic phase of limit-cycle oscillators

title: Variance Stable Gaussian Smoothing Estimator for Arbitrary High-order Derivatives
authors: Shuixin Fang, Xuerui Wang, Hang Zeng, Tao Zhou
abstract: Computing high-order partial derivatives in high dimensions by automatic differentiation can be costly in both computation and memory. Stein's identity offers an alternative through Gaussian smoothing, but the variance of the resulting estimators can diverge as the step size tends to zero, even with antithetic sampling. We propose a variance stabilization technique that extends antithetic sampling from a reflection pair to $n$ equally spaced points on a circle in the complex plane. Under local analyticity, we prove that, when $n$ is at least the derivative order, the bias is of order $O(σ^n)$ and the variance remains bounded as the smoothing step size $σ$ tends to zero. Numerical experiments support these predictions and demonstrate the effectiveness of the estimator in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for polyharmonic and Cahn--Hilliard equations. The technique mitigates the bias-variance trade-off in smoothing-based derivative estimation and is useful for PINNs solving high-order partial differential equations.

infographic.key_insight: Extending antithetic sampling to equally spaced complex-circle points stabilizes Gaussian-smoothed high-order derivative estimates as the smoothing step approaches zero.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The estimator offers an alternative to costly high-order automatic differentiation, with demonstrated use in PINNs for high-order PDEs.
method: Estimate derivatives through Gaussian smoothing and Stein’s identity.
Replace reflection pairs with n equally spaced points on a circle in the complex plane.
Under local analyticity and n at least the derivative order, obtain O(σ^n) bias and variance bounded as σ → 0.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments support the theoretical predictions and demonstrate effectiveness in PINNs for polyharmonic and Cahn–Hilliard equations.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees require local analyticity, and complex-valued function evaluations may complicate implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Variance Stable Gaussian Smoothing Estimator for Arbitrary High-order Derivatives

title: Func-JEPA: Learning a Sobolev Space of Functions as Latent Vectors
authors: Alejandro Moreno Arcas
abstract: Pretraining an encoder once and reusing it across tasks is a widespread approach in vision and language. However, neural symbolic mathematics still trains a dedicated sequence-to-sequence model for each task, so that no representation of a function is shared. In this work, we propose the Function Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Func-JEPA, abbreviated f-JEPA): an encoder of mathematical functions, pretrained on their symbolic form, whose latent space imitates the Sobolev space H^1 and in which differentiation is a learned latent operator. The norm of a latent is computed exactly from the function, whereas its direction is learned to match Sobolev angles. The frozen encoder is then reused by lightweight modules for decoding, composition, integration, and regression from samples. The representation and four downstream tasks are evaluated within and outside the pretraining distribution. f-JEPA recovers exact formulas from noisy samples more often than the compared symbolic-regression methods, whereas computer algebra and task-specific models remain stronger on standard integration and differential-equation benchmarks.

infographic.key_insight: Func-JEPA learns reusable latent representations of symbolic functions whose geometry imitates the Sobolev space H¹, with differentiation learned as a latent operator.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A shared, frozen function encoder could reduce the need to train separate end-to-end models for symbolic mathematics tasks.
method: Pretrain an encoder on symbolic functions.
Compute latent norms exactly from functions and learn directions to match Sobolev angles.
Reuse the frozen encoder with lightweight modules for decoding, composition, integration, and regression from samples.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated within and outside the pretraining distribution, f-JEPA recovers exact formulas from noisy samples more often than compared symbolic-regression methods, but trails computer algebra and task-specific models on standard integration and differential-equation benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The shared representation does not yet replace specialized solvers across symbolic mathematics tasks.
infographic.paper_title: Func-JEPA: Learning a Sobolev Space of Functions as Latent Vectors

title: Efficient Modeling of Multi-Agent Systems via Structure-Aware Physics-Informed Learning
authors: Yulun Wu, Nicola Bastianello, Karl Henrik Johansson, Matthieu Barreau
abstract: Modeling large multi-agent systems poses challenges for trajectory inference and parameter identification, as network size and coupling increase computational demands and partial observations require reconstructing unobserved states. We propose MAS-PINN, a neural-network architecture with a tailored training algorithm for a physics-informed learning framework that leverages the network topology and the agents' similarity to reduce computational and memory costs of simulating and identifying multi-agent systems. Its architecture represents agent trajectories through shared temporal features and agent-specific coefficients. Training alternates between learning features, fitting coupled trajectories, and estimating physical parameters. A matrix-free update exploits local interactions to fit trajectories without forming large global matrices. Experiments on Lorenz rings, Lotka--Volterra networks, and Rössler oscillators show improved trajectory and parameter accuracy over baselines, including inference in large systems and identification under partial observations or unknown topology, alongside substantial computational savings in coefficient fitting.

infographic.key_insight: MAS-PINN uses shared temporal features and network structure to learn multi-agent dynamics with lower computational and memory costs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports scalable trajectory reconstruction and physical-parameter identification in coupled systems with partially observed states.
method: Represent agent trajectories using shared temporal features and agent-specific coefficients.
Alternate feature learning, coupled-trajectory fitting, and physical-parameter estimation.
Exploit local interactions with matrix-free coefficient updates instead of large global matrices.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on Lorenz rings, Lotka–Volterra networks, and Rössler oscillators report improved trajectory and parameter accuracy over baselines, including partial-observation and unknown-topology settings, with substantial savings in coefficient fitting.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative speedups or error metrics, leaving practical gains for a target network to be verified.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Modeling of Multi-Agent Systems via Structure-Aware Physics-Informed Learning

title: Mean-field Token Steering
authors: Md Zulfiqur Haider, Asmaa Eldesoukey, Abhishek Halder, Yongxin Chen
abstract: We consider stochastic token steering through a deep stack of transformer layers as a mean-field control problem for an interacting particle system on the unit sphere, where interactions arise from the attention mechanism. In the mean-field limit, the token population evolves via a controlled integro-partial differential equation where the feedback control acts as a corrective vector field guiding the population toward an aggregate configuration of tokens in the representation space. We deduce the minimum effort control to accomplish this task over a fixed time horizon interpreted as normalized layer depth. We show that the resulting controlled dynamics for the token population can be understood as a mean-field Schrödinger bridge adapted to the sphere geometry. Building on this, we propose a novel generalization of the dynamic Sinkhorn recursion to compute the consistent token evolution. Numerical experiments confirm that the proposed approach achieves exact steering of the token population.

infographic.key_insight: Token steering across transformer layers is formulated as minimum-effort mean-field control on the unit sphere, yielding a geometry-aware Schrödinger bridge.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a principled way to guide aggregate token representations toward a target configuration over a fixed layer-depth horizon.
method: Model attention-coupled stochastic tokens as interacting particles on the unit sphere.
Derive a controlled mean-field integro-PDE and minimum-effort feedback field.
Generalize dynamic Sinkhorn recursion to compute consistent token evolution.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments report exact token-population steering, but the abstract provides no benchmark details or quantitative metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Scalability and steering accuracy for finite token populations in practical transformers remain unclear from the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Mean-field Token Steering

title: In-Context Estimation and Prediction for Parametric ODEs
authors: Abdullah Ahmed, Yun Yang
abstract: Transformers have demonstrated the ability to perform in-context learning, that is, to adapt to new tasks from a few examples without updating their parameters. Existing theory has largely focused on emulating gradient-based algorithms for convex statistical problems or establishing general function approximation guarantees without exploiting the underlying statistical structure. We study in-context parameter estimation and trajectory prediction for parametric ordinary differential equations (ODEs), where estimation is generally nonconvex. Under suitable identifiability and regularity conditions, we construct a transformer that estimates unknown system parameters from noisy trajectory observations through a two-stage approximate maximum likelihood procedure: a coarse search provides an initialization within a locally strongly convex region, followed by gradient descent with local linear contraction. For prediction, we compose this estimator with a neural approximation of the ODE solution map. We further show that, through parameter sharing, a single transformer can perform both parameter estimation and trajectory prediction simultaneously. For these constructions, we establish nonasymptotic guarantees and finite-pretraining oracle inequalities that separate errors due to finite pretraining data, finite context length, and finite-sized transformer approximation. Numerical experiments on linear and nonlinear ODEs further show that pretrained transformers can benefit from longer inference contexts without updating their weights.

infographic.key_insight: Under identifiability and regularity conditions, a transformer can estimate ODE parameters from noisy observations and predict trajectories in context without updating its weights.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a route to adapting dynamical-system models to new observations without retraining, potentially supporting system identification and forecasting.
method: Use coarse parameter search to initialize within a locally strongly convex region.
Refine estimates with gradient descent as part of approximate maximum likelihood estimation.
Compose the estimator with a neural ODE solution-map approximation, sharing parameters to support both tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper provides nonasymptotic guarantees and finite-pretraining oracle inequalities, while experiments on linear and nonlinear ODEs show benefits from longer inference contexts with fixed weights.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees require identifiability and regularity conditions; practical costs of coarse search and longer contexts need scrutiny.
infographic.paper_title: In-Context Estimation and Prediction for Parametric ODEs

title: Dimension-free spectral laws and the risk of spectral filters
authors: Chen Cheng
abstract: Spectral properties of the sample covariance are key to modern machine learning with high-dimensional data. Random matrix theory (RMT) supplies powerful tools; however, most classical results assume proportional asymptotics, where $d/n$ tends to a finite limit. In functional data analysis and kernel methods, a fixed infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is often the more natural setting for the observations, beyond the scope of proportional asymptotics. This calls for a dimension-free spectral theory for i.i.d. observations $\boldsymbol{x}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{x}_n$ in a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ with trace-class population covariance $Σ$. Building on the dimension-free ridge regression analysis of Cheng and Montanari (2024), we establish two deterministic equivalents with explicit nonasymptotic error bounds. The first approximates the empirical spectral law $\widehatμ_n$ of the sample Gram matrix by a deterministic law $μ_n$. The second characterizes the conditional prediction risk of analytic spectral filters in linear regression. Previous sharp approximations to prediction risk in this setting have focused on ridge regression and closely-related problems. Our analysis covers a broader class of filters at the bulk scale, with an explicit user-friendly spectral stability condition to check. We apply our theory to power and critical spectral laws, and we recover the proportional regime. For prediction, we study (negative) ridge estimators, iterated ridge, and gradient flow. Mathematically, building on the idea of stochastic interpolation, we construct a deterministic backward path to interpolate the spectral parameter. The resulting bounds on resolvent and mixed-resolvent traces give mesoscopic approximations to the spectral law within the bulk and, by Cauchy's formula, deterministic equivalents for the prediction variance and squared bias of analytic spectral filters.

infographic.key_insight: Dimension-free deterministic equivalents approximate sample covariance spectra and spectral-filter prediction risk, with explicit nonasymptotic error bounds beyond proportional asymptotics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The theory supports prediction-risk analysis for kernel and functional-data methods where observations naturally inhabit an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space.
method: Construct a deterministic backward path that interpolates the spectral parameter.
Bound resolvent and mixed-resolvent traces to approximate spectral laws within the bulk.
Apply Cauchy’s formula to derive prediction variance and squared bias for analytic spectral filters.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical applications to power and critical spectral laws, recovery of the proportional regime, and analysis of negative ridge, iterated ridge, and gradient flow—not empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Applicability requires checking the stated spectral stability condition; the filter analysis concerns analytic filters at the bulk scale, not arbitrary filters or spectral-edge behavior.
infographic.paper_title: Dimension-free spectral laws and the risk of spectral filters

title: Canonical activation patterns and ReLU pattern varieties
authors: Bella Finkel, Yaoying Fu, Chenxi Wu
abstract: A ReLU pattern variety records the polynomial relations among the coefficients of the affine maps associated with a prescribed set of activation patterns of a ReLU network. We study how the combinatorics of the canonical set of activation patterns of an unbiased ReLU network is reflected in the geometry of its pattern variety. In particular, we introduce the notion of pattern stability and characterize pattern stability and combinatorial stability for shallow networks. When the associated wall graph is connected and contains an edge of every neuron label, we resolve a problem of Alexandr and Montúfar by determining the defining ideal of the associated pattern variety explicitly. We establish a hierarchy of progressively weaker equivalence relations relating labeled combinatorial equivalence, equality and permutation equivalence of canonical pattern sets, and equivalences of the associated varieties. Finally, we relate functional dimension to the differential of the pattern map and show that it is bounded above by the dimension of the canonical pattern variety at every depth. For nondegenerate shallow networks, we give an exact formula for the functional dimension; for every shallow architecture, it equals the dimension of the canonical pattern variety on an open dense set of full Lebesgue measure.

infographic.key_insight: Canonical activation patterns link ReLU network combinatorics to algebraic geometry, with pattern-variety dimension bounding functional dimension at every depth.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results provide a theoretical framework for analyzing effective model capacity through activation structure rather than parameter counts alone.
method: Introduce pattern stability and characterize it alongside combinatorial stability for shallow networks.
Determine defining ideals when the wall graph is connected and includes every neuron label.
Relate functional dimension to the pattern-map differential and derive an exact formula for nondegenerate shallow networks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical guarantees, including equality of functional and canonical pattern-variety dimensions on an open dense, full-measure set for every shallow architecture, rather than empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The strongest exact characterizations require shallow networks or specific wall-graph conditions; the all-depth result is an upper bound.
infographic.paper_title: Canonical activation patterns and ReLU pattern varieties

title: A Staggered Discontinuous Galerkin Neural Network Method with a Computable Error Decomposition
authors: Gung-Min Gie, Chang-Yeol Jung, Bongsuk Kwon, Kiwoong Kwon
abstract: We develop a staggered discontinuous Galerkin neural network (SDGNN) method for scalar elliptic problems with a computable error decomposition. The staggered discontinuous Galerkin (SDG) method requires only local continuity of its trial functions and gives a square, inf-sup stable system without stabilization parameters; we carry this structure over to neural networks. Networks defined on the patches of a staggered mesh satisfy the SDG continuity conditions for all values of the network parameters, and the loss is the squared dual norm of the SDG weak residual. We show that the loss is equivalent, with computable constants, to the square of the training error, the distance between the SDG projection of the network and the SDG finite element approximation, so that the full error is bounded by the discretization error, a multiple of the square root of the loss, and the network projection error. The weak residual requires no derivatives of the networks, the boundary and convection terms carry no penalty or stabilization weights, and the scalar trial functions may jump across the midlines of the primal cells. Numerical experiments show that the square root of the loss tracks the error during the training, that prescribed jumps across a square and a circular interface are captured consistently over the initializations, and that the method is more accurate than physics-informed neural networks at the same parameter counts.

infographic.key_insight: SDGNN preserves staggered discontinuous Galerkin structure in neural networks and bounds total error by discretization, computable residual-based training, and network projection errors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For scalar elliptic problems, the method provides a computable training-error indicator without network derivatives or penalty and stabilization weights.
method: Use patchwise networks that satisfy SDG continuity conditions for every parameter choice.
Minimize the squared dual norm of the SDG weak residual.
Relate loss to training error through computable equivalence constants.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported numerical experiments show that square-root loss tracks error during training, prescribed square and circular interface jumps are captured consistently across initializations, and SDGNN outperforms PINNs at matched parameter counts.
infographic.watch_item: Low loss alone does not guarantee low total error; discretization and network projection errors also contribute.
infographic.paper_title: A Staggered Discontinuous Galerkin Neural Network Method with a Computable Error Decomposition

title: On the Convergence of Continuous-Time AdamW
authors: Bangjie Wang, Ning Ning
abstract: Continuous-time AdamW provides a framework for understanding whether an optimizer widely used to train large-scale neural networks settles to an equilibrium or sustains persistent motion. We study this long-time behavior while retaining bias correction and fixed positive weight decay. Under suitable assumptions, we establish that the dynamics are well defined for all time and remain bounded when the decay is sufficiently small. Our main result connects their limiting behavior to the geometry of the objective: trajectories approach a locally invariant manifold whose dimension equals the Hessian nullity along the associated critical component. When critical points are isolated and have at most one such direction, the trajectory converges to a single equilibrium. With two degenerate directions, however, bounded persistent motion can occur even for a smooth, strictly convex objective with a unique minimum. We also quantify how close the long-time trajectory remains to the critical set as weight decay decreases, without assuming convergence to a point. These results identify objective geometry as a key to understanding when continuous-time AdamW converges and when persistent motion is possible.

infographic.key_insight: Hessian degeneracy shapes continuous-time AdamW’s long-run behavior: isolated critical points with nullity at most one yield convergence, while two degenerate directions can permit bounded persistent motion.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results offer a geometric lens for reasoning about AdamW stability, showing that even strict convexity need not guarantee convergence in continuous time.
method: Analyze continuous-time AdamW with bias correction and fixed positive weight decay.
Establish global well-posedness and boundedness under suitable assumptions and sufficiently small decay.
Relate limiting dynamics to locally invariant manifolds whose dimension matches Hessian nullity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical guarantees, a persistent-motion example for a smooth strictly convex objective with a unique minimum, and bounds on long-time proximity to the critical set as decay decreases.
infographic.watch_item: These conditional continuous-time results do not directly establish convergence or instability for discrete AdamW implementations.
infographic.paper_title: On the Convergence of Continuous-Time AdamW
